did_you_know.text: In Genesis 1, humans are given plants for food, while here they are explicitly permitted to eat animals for the first time. The chapter thus describes a change in human diet after the Flood.
In the biblical world, blood was seen as carrying the power of life, which is why eating it was forbidden. This is a religious idea, not a description of modern biology.
This verse connects the prohibition against murder with the belief that every person is created in God’s image. It became a central foundation for the special value of human life.
Noah’s covenant includes not only human beings but also animals. The story therefore presents the entire living world as part of the responsibility that follows the Flood.
The Hebrew word keshet means both a weapon’s bow and a rainbow. The image places the bow in the sky as a sign connected with the end of destruction.
A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted, reflected, and dispersed inside water droplets in the air. That is why it is usually seen when sunlight and rain occur together.
Canaan is mentioned here before the story about Noah and his sons, preparing the reader for what follows in Genesis. Canaan will become central to many biblical stories as a land and a people.
The phrase “man of the soil” creates a wordplay with the Hebrew words for “Adam” and “ground.” Noah is portrayed as renewing the work of farming after the Flood.
Shem and Japheth cover their father while facing away so they will not look at him. Their action emphasizes honoring a parent and protecting his dignity when he is vulnerable.
The verse curses Canaan, Ham’s son, rather than Ham himself. This distinction matters because later people developed mistaken interpretations that applied the curse to all of Ham’s descendants.
